# InfiniGen: Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models with Dynamic KV Cache Management

## Abstract

InfiniGen is a KV cache management framework that improves performance and accuracy in long-text generation by pre-fetching essential KV cache entries in offloading-based LLM serving systems.

Generating long content with LLMs presents a challenge due to the substantial memory requirements of the transient state, known as the key-value (KV) cache, which scales with sequence length and batch size. This blog reviews InfiniGen, a novel KV cache management framework designed specifically for long-text generation, which integrates seamlessly with modern offloading-based inference systems, which leverage larger CPU memory. InfiniGen leverages a key insight: only a few essential tokens are [...] tokens are necessary to compute the attention layers of Transformers in subsequent steps. By speculating on these critical tokens using the inputs of the current layer and part of the query weight and key cache of the next layer, InfiniGen enables prefetching of only the essential KV cache entries, thus reducing fetch overhead from host CPU memory in offloading-based LLM systems. results.title: KV Cache Compression and Its Infra Problems | Efficient AI
results.content:
When a Transformer generates a token, it computes a query, a key, and a value vector; the new query attends over all previous keys and values to read the model's own history. The KV cache is what makes this affordable: each token's K and V are computed once and saved, and every later step reuses them instead of recomputing — O(n) work per step instead of O(n²). But nothing ever shrinks it: every generated token appends new K and V rows across all layers and heads. [...] Figure 1. Schematic, not to scale: every token the model generates appends its keys and values to the running history — the KV cache — so cache memory grows with output length while the weights stay fixed. Let generation run long enough, and the cache alone drives the GPU out of memory. [...] The hard part of KV cache compression is not choosing which tokens to keep — it is two collisions with production infrastructure. Existing methods need historical attention scores, but the FlashAttention kernel never writes those scores into GPU memory. And paged attention reclaims memory only when a block holds no KV at all — yet after token eviction the survivors leave almost every block partially occupied, so the "freed" memory never actually comes back.
